world.bio: I run the fungal herbarium at a university lab in Vancouver, which means I look after about 9,000 dried specimens and answer questions from anyone who sends a photo of a mushroom. Each autumn I do voucher identification for the poison control centre, and my lab review counts community outreach hours. Outside work I am training for a climbing trip to Squamish, fostering a senior dog and learning to bake sourdough.
skills_assets: Ten years of fungal taxonomy and microscopy experience, comfortable with spore prints, Melzer's reagent and a good key
The university herbarium: about 9,000 dried specimens, a cold room, and a good set of reference books
Voucher identification service for poison control, a standing arrangement each autumn
A DNA barcoding bench for ITS sequencing when the microscope is not enough
A university email account that gets forwarded photos of every mushroom someone's neighbour has eaten

projects.name: Autumn poison control vouchers
projects.text: Every autumn the poison control centre sends me vouchers from people who ate wild mushrooms and got sick. I identify them within 24 hours so the clinicians know what they are dealing with. This year there have already been eleven, mostly Amanita and a few Galerina lookalikes. It is a quiet kind of high-stakes work.

projects.name: Lab annual review
projects.text: Our annual review asks each of us to log community outreach hours. I am at 6 out of a target of 20, and the other staff are well past that. My manager has gently reminded me twice.

projects.name: Climbing training for Squamish
projects.text: Trip in November with a friend, three days on the Chief. I am training at the gym twice a week and doing hangboard sessions in my kitchen, which my dog finds suspicious.

notes.text: Three vouchers on the bench this morning. One was clearly a young Amanita phalloides, the others were harmless but the senders did not know. I spent an hour with the microscope and then called the poison centre with results. Someone is being monitored at VGH tonight. It is in moments like these I remember why this job matters.

Fostering a ten-year-old beagle called Biscuit. She sleeps eighteen hours a day and snores like a small outboard motor. I was supposed to have her only for two weeks and it has been four. I think I am not giving her back.

First attempt at sourdough ended up as a brick. The starter smelled like nail polish remover. My friend said that means it is hungry. I fed it three times today and it still smells like a chemistry lab. Which, to be fair, is where I work.

Manager reminded me again about outreach hours. I have done a few talks for school groups but those do not seem to add up. She said, 'Maybe do something regular, something that counts.' I nodded, but I have no idea what. I do not like crowds, and I have very little free time in autumn.
Hangboard session in the kitchen. Hung for seven seconds, ten seconds, then my fingers gave. Biscuit looked at me from the couch as if I was losing my mind. Maybe I am.

Spent the evening cataloguing a batch of chanterelles brought in by a citizen scientist. Beautiful specimens, perfectly dried. Wrote the labels in my neatest handwriting. It is a small pleasure, making sure a specimen will be useful for the next fifty years.
Mum called. She wants me to come for Thanksgiving. I said I would see. She said 'you always say you will see.' She is right.
Walked Biscuit around Pacific Spirit Park. We passed a patch of Hericium on a maple log. I took a photo and sent it to the lab group chat. Three people replied with exclamation marks.
Drove up to Squamish for a day to scope the approach. Rain, fog, cold. But the Chief looked impossibly huge. I stood there and thought, I am going to be scared and I am going to do it anyway.

messages.text:
Okafor: Mei-Ling, we've got another one, photo attached. Any chance you can look at it today?
Me: Sending it to the microscope right now. Give me two hours.
Okafor: You're a lifesaver, literally.

Rachel: Mei-Ling, the outreach hours. We need to be at 20 by December.
Me: I know. I am working on it.
Rachel: Maybe a regular community thing? Something that shows up on the log.

Sam: Still on for the Chief in November?
Me: Yes, I'm training. Two sessions a week.
Sam: Good. I'll book the campsite.

Mum: Thanksgiving, are you coming?
Me: I'll let you know next week.
Mum: You always say that.
Me: Mum.

Neighbour: Is it OK to eat these? (photo of mushrooms)
Me: Please don't. They look like a Galerina. Bring them to the lab and I'll check.

relations.about: Warm, direct, depends on her ID calls
Supportive but firm about the outreach hours
Reliable partner on rope, a bit reckless on routes
Lives in Burnaby, wants her at family dinners

constraints: Voucher work is confidential and tied to patient safety; I cannot share case details
Weekdays are busy; evenings and weekends are more flexible
No time to lead a public workshop series by herself
I will not identify mushrooms from photos for people to eat
sensitive: Feels burnt out some autumn weeks, the poison control calls weigh on her
Tension with her mother over holidays
Money is fine but her lab contract is year to year
